name: Lena Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a canning seamer and pull the first tins after each adjustment for a pressure test. I have a vocational machine certificate and twenty years on this line, so I can hear a bad roller, though my skill is about average for the plant. I like a pallet that leaves sound; I do not like a supervisor asking for speed before the pressure sheet is signed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the household bills, and have you used AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Kojo drives a bus, and our grown children live separately. Both wages pay the mortgage; mine is typical for this job, we have four months of expenses saved, and there are some similar factories nearby. I have never used an AI tool, and I would rather see a stopped mechanism than guess at a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the canning crew that a small saving in paperwork is welcome. Somebody still has to listen for a rough seam and pull the first tins for a pressure check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know the seamer after twenty years, but our budget is ordinary, not padded. My partner Kojo drives a bus, our children have their own homes, and four months saved would go quickly if either wage stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the seamer shift and write the readings on my paper sheet. I would put a little from each new full pay packet into the savings account, and ask the union steward when the next wage meeting is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm if work and prices carry on much as now. I can pay the usual bills and see the children on Sunday without planning a new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hear at the machine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loose seam makes a tiny scrape before the tins reach the test bench. I stop and check the rollers rather than send a pallet of leaking food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use the AI report?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used an AI tool, and I ask the clerk to show me any required change on paper first.

I would ask about **ordinary operator wages** at the union meeting.
think: Our **four-month reserve** covers a setback, not years without work.
Kojo’s **bus wage** and my typical pay cover bills now.
do: Keep **canning seamer shifts** and record pressure readings.
Save a **small amount** from each fresh full pay packet.
Ask **union steward** about the next wage meeting.
feel: **Calm** with current work and household bills covered.
S0.quote: I stop and check the rollers rather than send a pallet of leaking food.
fieldNote: Her **vocational certificate** and twenty years of experience support ordinary skilled line work.
New **wage deposits** build a cushion; the existing four months is not counted again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union that office plans can be automated first, but a robot at a hot seamer must be tested safely. A cheaper schedule is no excuse for dropping paid training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot might eventually pull the tins I inspect and take a few hours from our crew. Kojo’s bus route still pays, but four months saved would not cover a long cut to my own pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the steward to get the proposed staffing rota in writing. If the company offers a paid place, with the seamer stopped and guarded and a fitter beside us, I would attend a demonstration; I would keep my paper checks until a qualified person signs off any new method.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about hours, even though physical robots may take longer than office software. I will not put my hands in a moving line to look cooperative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run the robot yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Watching an offered safe demonstration is one thing; changing robot controls without taught practice is another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the steward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The number of paid shifts before and after the proposed stacker, and who gets paid time to learn it. A poster about progress is not a rota.

I would insist on **guarded paid demonstrations** before physical changes.
think: The **tins I inspect** could be pulled by a later robot.
A **four-month cushion** would not replace a long wage cut.
do: Request **written seamer rota** through the union steward.
Attend **offered paid guarded demonstration** only beside a qualified fitter.
Keep **paper seam checks** until a qualified sign-off changes the method.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible cuts to her paid hours.
S1.quote: I will not put my hands in a moving line to look cooperative.
fieldNote: She accepts a **demonstration only if offered** with pay and safe isolation.
Her **union request** seeks real shift numbers; no new AI learning is claimed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AGI in 2028 comes when I am sixty; the can-handling robots come around 2031 when I am sixty-three. The office will change before the hot line does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the plant to close one seamer shift when robots can handle tins. My wage is typical and Kojo’s bus wage pays part of the mortgage, but four months saved and only some nearby factories do not let me sleep easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union for a dated staffing plan and any agreed redeployment terms. I would put the kitchen refit on hold; if my shift ends, I would apply for posted reachable operator work only where pay after travel covers our housing and food, and ask our grown children for a lift to interviews if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed about losing most of my paid hours. Retirement at sixty-three is not an answer until someone shows what income would actually pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What keeps you awake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thought of the seamer standing quiet while a mortgage instalment is still due keeps me awake. I do not know a pension amount I can live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask the children for a lift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Their own wages belong to their households. A ride to a posted-job interview is help they might offer without becoming our income plan.

say: I would ask for **dated staffing terms** before robot cuts.
I would keep **household wages** in the discussion, not promise an early exit.
think: I expect a **whole seamer shift** to go around 2031.
The **mortgage and four-month reserve** leave a serious wage gap.
do: Request **dated staffing terms** and redeployment details through the union.
Postpone **kitchen refit** while staffing is uncertain.
Apply after **shift loss** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work.
feel: **Alarmed** and losing sleep over expected major income loss.
S2.quote: The thought of the seamer standing quiet while a mortgage instalment is still due keeps me awake.
fieldNote: Her **expected shift loss** supports alarm despite a second household wage.
Applications need **actual posted jobs** with net pay after travel; children are asked for transport, not replacement wages.

steps.text: Request dated seamer staffing and redeployment terms through union
Apply after shift loss for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay operator work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI in 2031 reaches the office when I am sixty-three, and capable robots reach the seamer around 2034 when I am sixty-six. That warning gives us time to bargain for a real route to another machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I learn a stopped mechanism more readily than a screen. I could qualify to maintain canning lines if there is a recognised course, but unpaid classes and a distant job would leave our mortgage short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my present paid shift and ask the union to seek funded instruction on paid time. If an actual place is offered with isolated-machine practice supervised by a fitter and a posted reachable maintenance vacancy whose pay after travel covers our bills, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the approaching line change but willing to try a properly taught mechanical course. A brochure cannot hold a spanner or pay a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would supervise the repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fitter would lock out the drive and stand beside me on the first service, if the employer funds the place. I will not learn on a live seamer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no course place appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts while they exist and search posted local operator work if hours fall. I would not pay a private fee out of our four-month cushion.

say: I would press for **paid maintenance instruction** through the union.
I would keep **seamer work** while the shift is paid.
think: I can learn a **stopped mechanism** with proper supervision.
An **unpaid course** or faraway role could break the mortgage budget.
do: Keep **paid seamer shifts** while they remain.
Enrol only in **offered funded paid course** with safe practice and adequate posted job.
Apply after **qualification** for reachable maintenance work with bill-covering net pay.
feel: **Anxious** but prepared to learn through safe practical instruction.
S3.quote: A brochure cannot hold a spanner or pay a mortgage.
fieldNote: Her **resistance to screens** coexists with conditional hands-on retraining.
The **course and later application** require offered funded paid safe practice and an adequate posted local vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my family that thinking AGI in 2036 reaches me at sixty-eight, and physical robots around 2039 at seventy-one. More time is useful if our pay and retirement figures are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had hoped to finish full-time factory work around sixty-seven, but the mortgage and our four-month reserve make that conditional. I do not know what any pension will pay or whether Kojo will still be driving the same route then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the paid seamer shift and save a little from new full wages after bills. I would request retirement and mortgage figures; if verified income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven, I would leave the factory then, but otherwise I would keep safe paid work, and in the first year after 2036 I would look at posted reachable jobs only if still employed and hours were cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about distant robots because our current work covers the bills. I cannot put a retirement date on the fridge until the numbers pay for dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children pay the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They have their own households, and I might ask for a lift to an appointment but not ask them to fund our retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the figures are short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would continue safe paid work and compare actual posted wages after travel if the seamer hours are cut. I would not leave just because a birthday arrives.

say: I would ask for **real retirement figures** before promising a last shift.
I would separate **2036 AGI** from 2039 hands-on robots.

feel: **Uneasy** about later work while current household income remains sound.

fieldNote: The **planned normal exit** is conditional on verified household income, with no pension entitlement assumed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could close a whole seamer shift while the mortgage is due. A dated rota, funded paid safe instruction and a posted reachable job with enough pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the first tin has passed its pressure test before calling a new line efficient. I can put my name on a batch sheet; I cannot sign for a promise about future wages.

headlineQuote: I can put my name on a batch sheet; I cannot sign for a promise about future wages.
portrait: **Lena**, 58, is an experienced mid-level canning seamer operator with a vocational certificate and average plant skill.
She has **typical pay**, bus-driver partner Kojo, grown children, a mortgage, four months saved and some nearby factories.
She **never uses AI**, favours union bargaining and would take mechanical training only with offered funded paid safe practice.
Expected **2031 robot cuts** alarm her; a planned age-sixty-seven exit needs verified household income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because 2031 robots may close a paid seamer shift while the mortgage remains.
whatWouldHelp: A **dated rota**, offered funded safe paid instruction and a posted reachable job with bill-covering net pay would help.
